At 5-year follow up, 97.7 % of implants (95 % CI: 91.2 to 99.4) were free from revision or removal with 84 implants at risk. These researchers recorded 2 cases (2.3 %) of failure for septic loosening. The authors concluded that trans-fibular TAA was safe and effective with a high survival rate at mid-term follow-up and satisfactory clinical and radiological results. Moreover, these researchers stated that further studies are needed to determine the long-term performance of these implants. Day et al (2025) noted that while most TAA procedures employ an anterior approach for implantation, the Zimmer Biomet Trabecular Metal implant is unique in that it uses lateral trans-fibular approach. In a retrospective study, these researchers presented the largest mid-term study to-date to analyze the implant survivorship and clinical and radiographic outcomes of trans-fibular TAA at a minimum 5-year follow-up. These investigators examined 130 ankles (122 patients; mean age of 60.8 years; 50 % women) with a mean follow-up of 5.9 years (range of 5.0 to 10.1 years) after primary TAA performed between October 2012 and December 2018. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) included the 12-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-12) Physical Component Summary (PCS) and Mental Component Summary (MCS), AOS for pain and disability, and VAS for pain. Radiographic measurements for ROM, coronal and sagittal alignment, and implant subsidence were evaluated. The presence of peri-prosthetic radiolucency was determined using a 12-zone classification system. Adverse events (AEs) were reported using the Canadian Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society (COFAS) Reoperation Coding System (CROCS). The cohort had mean post-operative values of 41.5 for the SF-12 PCS, 54.9 for the SF-12 MCS, 2.3 for VAS pain, 19.1 for AOS pain, and 28.5 for AOS disability. The post-operative tibio-talar ROM was 7.5° of dorsiflexion and 17.3° of plantar flexion. A total of 42 valgus ankles (mean coronal tibio-talar angle of 10.4°; range of 1.0° to 25.3°) and 44 varus ankles (mean of -9.1°; range of -1.0° to -25.0°) were corrected to neutral. A total of 26 ankles (20 %) had 1 zone of radiolucency, and none of the ankles had greater than 7 zones. There were 3 cases of cysts (2.3 %) and 0 cases of subsidence, septic or aseptic loosening, or fibular nonunion. AEs occurred in 47 ankles (36.2 %) at a mean of 26.7 months, with the most common re-operation being medial gutter debridement (22 ankles; 16.9 %). There were 2 ankles (1.5 %) with acute infection treated with debridement, antibiotics, and polyethylene exchange with metal component retention. Overall implant survivorship, defined as retention of the metal components, was 100 % at the time of final follow-up. The authors concluded that clinical and radiographic data in this study suggested that trans-fibular TAA was an effective and durable therapeutic option for end-stage ankle OA, with excellent mid-term implant survivorship. Peri-prosthetic radiolucency was limited and did not result in implant subsidence or loosening. The most common re-operation was medial gutter debridement. Level of Evidence = III. Patient-Specific Instrumentation in Total Ankle Arthroplasty Wang et al (2021) stated that patient-specific instrument (PSI) may theoretically make TAA more accurate. Several studies have reported the outcomes of PSI TAA. In a systematic review, these investigators examined the literature of PSI TAA. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases were systematically reviewed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines for PSI TAA. The quality of the included studies was evaluated according to Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS). A total of 9 studies were included in the systematic review. The implant position and function outcome of TAA was similar between PSI and standard instrumentation (SI). Prediction accuracy of implant size remained great difference. PSI could shorten the operative time and fluoroscopy time. These researchers stated that the quality of current studies on PSI TAA is insufficient to produce high-level evidence. The authors concluded that PSI could get similar implant position and clinical outcome in TAA compared to SI; however, current evidence is not strong enough to evaluate PSI TAA. Heisler et al (2022) noted that existing literature on the superiority of PSI in TAA over standard referencing (SR) is limited. Advantages presented include better implant alignment, shorter operating times, and increased accuracy of implant size prediction. In a retrospective study, these investigators examined PSI in the hands of an experienced foot and ankle surgeon new to both PSI and SR for this specific implant, in regard to determining implant alignment, operative times, and radiologic short-term outcome and predicting implant size for tibial and talar components. A total of 24 patients undergoing TAA using PSI were compared to 25 patients using SR instrumentation. Outcome measures included alignment of the tibial component (α coronal plane, γ sagittal plane), the tibiotalar tilt (β), and the talar offset x on the sagittal view as well as the presence of radiolucent lines, operation time, and wound healing. Post-operative outcome was assessed at 6 weeks, 4 months, and 1 year post-operatively. Implant positioning was similar in both groups, and no advantage in regard to the operative time could be observed when comparing TAA using PSI to SR. Implant size prediction was more reliable for the tibia than for the talus. Three patients (1 from the SR group and 2 from the PSI group) showed radiolucent lines around the tibial component; 2 patients (both SR group) suffered delayed wound healing, albeit not requiring any additional measures. The authors concluded that the findings of this trial suggested that PSI does not yet provide any meaningful initial advantage in the standard TAR when it comes to the accuracy of coronal or sagittal positioning for both tibial and talar component positioning. This is also the case for implant size estimation and operative time. Furthermore, these researchers observed, in line with a previous study, a trend to worse osteointegration/radiolucent lines; however, further investigation is needed to examine if this can be corroborated in a bigger cohort and for a longer follow-up. Level of Evidence = III. The authors stated that the major drawback of this trial was the method of the radiologic assessment of the ankle joints. These researchers followed the principles established in previous studies. As the shape of the tibia varies considerably, assessment of angles around the ankle joint on ankle radiographs does not appear very reliable. Ideally, the alignment should be examined on images including the ankle, the knee, and the hip joint. This is not the case in routine radiographs, leading to the necessity to perform a post-hoc correction in the PSI group. However, the assessment of the radiologic parameters themselves remains a manual process and is affected by observer variation. The 2 observers involved in this study showed a sufficiently low inter-observer variability to be able to regard their measurements on the post-surgical images as reliable. Second, one of the great advantages of PSI may be the determination of the rotation of the implant; however, this parameter was not examined in this trial. Furthermore, the cohort evaluated in this trial included the first patients receiving an Infinity TAA by the senior author. It has been postulated that PSI supports the surgeon in becoming familiar with a new implant. This would imply higher accuracy of the implant positioning in the PSI group, which, however, was not observed in this study. In additional, the patients in this cohort were not randomized. Radiographic parameters measured on the pre-operative radiographs retrospectively showed a trend that challenging cases were more often treated with PSI and straightforward cases with SR. Last but not least, the extra costs of PSI were not covered by health insurance, unless the patients have private insurance. Thus, the latter group was more likely to have access to the PSI method. However, at the end, it was the surgeon’s choice as to which method was employed. Mazzotti et al (2022) stated that the recent increase in the adoption of TAA reflects the improvements in implant designs and surgical techniques, including the use of pre-operative navigation system and PSI, such as custom-made cutting guides. Cutting guides are customized with respect to each patient's anatomy based on pre-operative ankle computed tomography (CT) scans, and they drive the saw intra-operatively to improve the accuracy of bone resection and implant positioning. Despite some promising results, the main queries in the literature are whether PSI improves the reliability of achieving neutral ankle alignment and more accurate implant sizing, whether it is actually superior over standard techniques, and whether it is cost-effective. Moreover, the advantages of PSI in clinical outcomes are still theoretical because the current literature does not allow to confirm its superiority. These researchers noted that the insufficiency of corroborating literature and scarcity of studies (in 2 cases financed by the manufacturer) represent the current and main drawbacks of PSI. Moreover, it is unclear if PSI may be more useful in order to restore ankle neutral alignment when dealing with complex deformities involving the whole lower limb. The authors concluded that further prospective, randomized, and multi-center studies are needed to better evaluate PSI and confirm its routine use in TAA. Total Ankle Replacement versus Ankle Arthrodesis for Patients Aged 50 to 85 Years with End-Stage Ankle Osteoarthritis In a multi-center, parallel-group, non-blinded, randomized controlled trial (RCT), Goldberg et al (2023) compared the clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and complication rates of TAR with those of arthrodesis (i.e., ankle fusion) in the treatment of end-stage ankle OA. Patients with end-stage ankle OA who were aged 50 to 85 years and were suitable for both procedures were recruited from 17 U.K. hospitals and randomized using minimization. The primary outcome was the change in the Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire walking/standing domain scores between the pre-operative baseline and 52 weeks post-surgery. Between March 2015 and January 2019, a total of 303 participants were randomized using a minimization algorithm: 152 to TAR and 151 to ankle fusion. At 52 weeks, the mean (standard deviation) Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire walking/standing domain score was 31.4 (30.4) in the TAR arm (n = 136) and 36.8 (30.6) in the ankle fusion arm (n = 140); the adjusted difference in the change was -5.6 (95 % CI: -12.5 to 1.4; p = 0.12) in the intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. By week 52, 1 patient in the TAR arm required revision. Rates of wound-healing issues (13.4 % versus 5.7 %) and nerve injuries (4.2 % versus less than 1 %) were higher and the rate of thrombo-embolic events was lower (2.9 % versus 4.9 %) in the TAR arm than in the ankle fusion arm. The bone non-union rate (based on plain radiographs) in the ankle fusion arm was 12.1 %, but only 7.1 % of patients had symptoms. A post-hoc analysis of fixed-bearing TAR showed a statistically significant improvement over ankle fusion in Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire walking/standing domain score (-11.1, 95 % CI: -19.3 to -2.9; p = 0.008). These researchers estimated a 69 % likelihood that TAR was cost-effective compared with ankle fusion at the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)'s cost-effectiveness threshold of £20,000 per quality-adjusted life-year gained over the patient's lifetime. The authors concluded that both TAR and ankle fusion improved patients' QOL at 1 year, and both appeared to be safe. When TAR was compared with ankle fusion overall, these investigators were unable to show a statistically significant difference between the 2 arms in terms of the primary outcome measure. The total ankle replacement versus ankle arthrodesis (TARVA) trial was inconclusive in terms of superiority of TAR, as the 95 % CI for the adjusted treatment effect included both a difference of 0 and the minimal important difference of 12, but it could rule out the superiority of ankle fusion. A post-hoc analysis comparing fixed-bearing TAR with ankle fusion showed a statistically significant improvement of TAR over ankle fusion in Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire walking/standing domain score. Total ankle replacement appeared to be cost-effective compared with ankle fusion at the NICE cost-effectiveness threshold of £20,000 per quality-adjusted life-year gained over a patient's lifetime based on long-term economic modelling. This study had several drawbacks. This initial report contained only 52-week data, which must therefore be interpreted with caution. In addition, the pragmatic nature of the study meant that there was heterogeneity between surgical implants and techniques. The Trial was run across 17 NHS center to ensure that decision-making streams reflected the standard of care in the NHS as closely as possible. Ankle Arthrodesis Versus Total Ankle Arthroplasty for the Treatment of End-Stage Ankle Arthritis In a systematic review, Zhou et al (2023) examined the effectiveness of TAA and AA in the treatment of end-stage ankle arthritis (ESAA). These investigators searched PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library databases for studies published in the treatment of ESAA with AA or TAA from inception to June 2021. Bias risk tool was used to evaluate the quality of the literature. The AOFAS, VAS, AOS, gait analysis (pace, frequency, stride), ROM, satisfaction, complications as well as re-operation rate were analyzed by meta-analysis between AA and TAA groups by RevMan 5.3 software. A total of 12 studies were included, including 1,050 patients in the AA group and 3,760 patients in the TAA group, totaling 4,810 patients. Meta-analysis showed that the total score of AOFAS (MD = -3.12, 95 % CI: -9.02 to 2.96, p = 0.31), pain score (MD = 1.60, 95 % CI: -1.35 to 4.54, p = 0.29], alignment score (MD = -0.04, 95 % CI: -0.52 to 0.44, p = 0.88], VAS (MD = 0.10, 95 % CI: -0.49 to 0.68), p = 0.74), and AOS total score (MD = -4.01, 95 % CI: -8.28 to 0.25, p = 0.06], the difference was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). The score of AOFAS functional in TAA group was significantly higher than that in TAA group (MD = 44.22, 95 % CI: -8.01 to -0.43, p = 0.03]. There was no significant difference in gait analysis between the 2 groups (p > 0.05). Post-operative ROM (MD = -4.93, 95 % CI: -6.35, to -3.52, p < 0.000 01] and change in ROM from pre-operative to follow-up (MD = -5.74, 95 % CI: -8.88 to -2.61, p = 0.0003) between 2 groups, the difference was statistically significant. There was no significant difference in satisfaction between the 2 groups (OR = 1.011, 95 % CI: 0.46 to 2.23, p = 0.98]. Complications (OR = 1.61, 95 % CI: 1.26 to 2.06, p = 0.0002] and non-revision re-operation (OR = 1.61, 95 % CI: 1.17 to 2.21, p = 0.003] were significantly lower in the TAA group than in the AA group. There was no significant difference in the rate of revision and re-operation (p > 0.05) between the 2 groups (OR = 1.02, 95 % CI: 0.37 to 2.78, p = 0.97). The authors concluded that the effectiveness of AA was similar to that of TAA; however, the non-revision re-operation rate and main surgical complications of TAA were significantly reduced; thus, further high-quality methodological research and long-term follow-up are needed to confirm this conclusion. Glazebrook et al (2024) noted that ESAA causes pain and dysfunction; and it is treated with TAA or AA. There is currently no consensus on which surgical procedure is superior. In a systematic review, these investigators examined high-quality studies directly comparing TAA and AA for the treatment of ESAA to determine superiority. They carried out a comprehensive literature review of the highest quality studies published that directly compared clinical outcomes of TAA and AA for the treatment of ESAA. Each study was assigned a Level of Evidence (LOE) rating (I to III) and then summarized to assign a grade of recommendation (A to C, I). Superiority was determined for the clinical outcomes of pain, activity, health related QOL (HR-QOL), re-admission to hospital, revision surgery, as well as general complications. There was fair evidence (GOR B) that supported both TAA and AA for the treatment of ESAA. However, TAA trended to be superior for pain relief (GOR B), activity (GOR B), HR-QOL (GOR B) and re-admission rate (GOR B) while AA trended to be superior for revision rates (GOR B). Conflicting evidence was presented for general complications (GOR C). The authors concluded that due to the lack of Level I studies as well as inconsistent findings, no definitive conclusion on which procedure is better can be made. However, there was adequate evidence to provide a basis for which procedure is more effective in each of the outcomes reviewed. This should be considered when deciding on which procedure is best suited for a patient on a case-by-case basis. These researchers stated that to allow for a stronger recommendation, further studies especially high-quality Level I RCTs directly comparing AA and TAA are needed. Level of Evidence = III. Corticosteroid Injection Prior to Ankle Arthroplasty Uçkay et al. (2019) published consensus recommendations regarding two questions: 1) Does intra-articular injection of the ankle with corticosteroids increase the risk of subsequent periprosthetic Joint Infection (PJI) following total ankle arthroplasty (TAA)?; 2) If so, how long after a prior intra-articular injection can total ankle arthroplasties (TAA) be safely performed? The group recommended that every intra-articular injection of the ankle is an invasive procedure associated with potential healthcare-associated infections, including periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) following total ankle arthroplasty (TAA). Based on the limited current literature, the ideal timing for elective TAA after corticosteroid injection for the symptomatic native ankle joint is unknown. The consensus workgroup recommends that at least 3 months pass after corticosteroid injection and prior to performing TAA (Level of evidence: Limited; Delegate vote: agree: 92%, disagree: 8%, abstain: 0% (super majority, strong consensus). Incisional Negative Pressure Wound Therapy Applied After Total Ankle Arthroplasty Atfeh et al (2025) stated that portable, single-use incisional negative pressure wound therapy (iNPWT) device could be used directly on the wound incision following TAA. In a single-center, single-surgeon study, these researchers carried out a three-dimensional (i.e., clinical, economic, and organizational) hospital based-health technology assessment (HB-HTA) to support local decision-making in a French university hospital for the adoption of iNPWT. The HB-HTA was based on a literature review; results from the PICO-PTC single-center RCT; and semi-structured interviews with healthcare professionals. Two comparative retrospective cohort studies were retrieved from the literature review, which suggested a decreased incidence of wound healing complications with iNPWT compared to standard dressings, although no difference was found in the PICO-PTC Trial. There was no significant difference in the PICO-PTC Trial on Medicine-Surgery-Obstetrics (MSO) hospital costs between the 2 strategies: €10,639.65 (95 % CI: 7,997.45 to 17,988.68) in the iNPWT group versus €9,672.59 (95 % CI: 7,966.29 to 13,393.65) in the standard dressings group. Adoption of this prophylactic strategy would result in an approval to pay a 1.5 % supplement to the MSO hospitalization costs. It could also improve professionals' work-flow, and facilitate wound healing monitoring for nurses in orthopedic departments compared to standard dressings. The authors concluded that the clinical effectiveness of iNPWT compared to standard dressings could not be demonstrated, in terms of the incidence of wound healing complications, in patients scheduled for TAA and not selected on the basis of risk factors. Moreover, these researchers stated that a larger study, with a “number-needed-to-treat” computed on the basis of incidence of complications in this indication is needed to show a clinical benefit of iNPWT compared to standard dressings, and to provide the clinical dimension of the HB-HTA report. They noted that a U.S. RCT (ClinicalTrial.gov identifier NCT05064696) with wound complications as the primary end-point and an estimated enrolment of 150 subjects is currently ongoing, and could provide an answer in the near future. Simultaneous Bilateral Scandinavian Total Ankle Arthroplasty Aitchison et al (2025) stated that TAR is an established treatment for end-stage ankle arthritis, offering pain relief and improved functionality. The Scandinavian Total Ankle Replacement (STAR) was 1st employed in the U.S. in 1998 and although unilateral STAR has been extensively studied, there is limited documentation on the outcomes of simultaneous bilateral STAR procedures. In a retrospective, single-center, case-series study, these researchers examined the survivability and PROMs of simultaneous bilateral STAR, focusing on implant survival rates, improvements in QOL, function, as well as pain relief. This trial was carried out on all patients managed with primary TAR carried out simultaneously with bilateral STAR prostheses at the authors’ institution from July 1998 to February 2008. Demographics and peri-operative characteristics were collected. Poisson regression was employed for analyzing implant survivability, and generalized linear mixed models were used to examine PROMs, including the VAS, SMFA, SF-36, and (AOFAS hind-foot, at multiple follow-up time-points. A total of 21 patients were included for a total of 42 implants. The average length of follow-up was 4.9 ± 2.7 years. The implant failure rate at 5 years was 12.0 % (95 % CI: 4.5 % to 32.0 %). The last recorded failure occurred at 8 years post-implant, with an implant failure rate of 19.2 % (95 % CI: 17.2 % to 51.1 %). Statistically significant improvements were observed in all PROMs from baseline to the 5-year follow-up (p < 0.05) except SMFA bother because of high variability and small sample size. The authors concluded that at mid-term follow-up, patients who underwent bilateral simultaneous TAR with the STAR prosthesis exhibited a significant and durable improvement in PROMs scores across multiple functional indices. Failure rates were within range to those reported in previous studies assessing unilateral STAR, with an estimated average survivorship of 80.8 % at 8 years. Level of Evidence = IV. The authors stated that this trial had several drawbacks. First, It is recognized that subsequent modifications to implant design and surgical technique may have been made since this original cohort underwent bilateral TAR with STAR implants. The sample size was relatively small (n = 21 patients), and the follow-up duration varied among patients. It was possible that earlier cases in the cohort were subject to higher failure rates because of the learning curve associated with TAR procedures. However, no correlation between failures and early-phase surgeries was observed in this study, even though this phenomenon has been reported in other early STAR cohorts. Second, given this was a single-center study, the results may not be generalizable to all patient populations. Third, these researchers did not systematically record minor complications such as wound healing problems or implant-associated fractures. Fourth, the retrospective nature of this trial introduced potential biases related to data collection and reporting. Because this was a historical cohort, these investigators employed legacy PROM instruments (VAS, SMFA, SF-36, AOFAS). Current practice often employs Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) measures, which may provide additional precision in evaluating foot and ankle function. These researchers stated that future, prospective studies with larger cohorts, validated PROMs, and longer follow-up periods are needed to validate these findings and further examine the long-term outcomes of bilateral STAR. In addition, bilateral TAR should be evaluated in a gait laboratory to compare its effects with both unilateral TAR and cases of ankle arthritis without joint replacement. There is currently a lack of data regarding how ankle joint mechanics, both before and after TAR, impact the ankle joint and the forces experienced by the hip and knee. Effect of Glycemic Control on Total Ankle Arthroplasty Good glycemic control improves outcomes of total ankle arthroplasty in persons with diabetes mellitus. Patients with uncontrolled diabetes experience significantly higher rates of clinical failure, infection, and wound complications compared to those with controlled diabetes or no diabetes (Choi, et al., 2014). A study of 173 patients undergoing TAA found that uncontrolled diabetic patients had significantly poorer outcomes than non-diabetic patients, with a 21% clinical failure rate in diabetics versus 11.6% in non-diabetics at mean 5-year follow-up (Choi, et al., 2014). The uncontrolled diabetic subgroup specifically demonstrated higher rates of delayed wound healing and early-onset osteolysis (Choi, et al., 2014). Large database studies confirm these findings, showing that diabetic patients have elevated rates of infection and wound dehiscence at both 90 and 365 days postoperatively, with insulin-dependent diabetes conferring 6.47-fold increased odds of infection within 30 days (Patel, et al., 2025; Qureshi, et al., 2024). Preoperative hemoglobin A1c levels directly correlate with complication risk. Each 1% increase in HbA1c increases the odds of developing a complication by 5% after elective foot and ankle surgery (Domek, et al., 2016). Patients with preoperative HbA1c >6.7% have a 9-fold increased risk of wound complications following total joint arthroplasty, and an HbA1c >7.45% significantly increases the likelihood of postoperative hyperglycemia >200 mg/dL (Stryker, et al., 2015; Godshaw, et al., 2018). Meta-analyses demonstrate that diabetic patients undergoing TAA face higher revision rates, postoperative infection rates, 30-day readmission rates, and longer hospital stays compared to non-diabetic patients (Fan, et al., 2025). The 5-year cumulative incidence of periprosthetic joint infection is 7.3% in diabetic patients versus 3.9% in non-diabetic patients (Helbing, et al., 2024). These findings support coordinated preoperative optimization and perioperative glycemic control as essential strategies to improve outcomes (Tarabichi, et al., 2023; Stryker, 2016).
